entry: Capital city of New York State (pop., 2020: 99,224), on the west bank of the [[Hudson River]]. Albany is the county seat of Albany County and the oldest city in New York. Dutch colonists built Fort Nassau in 1614 for fur trading, and the English took over in 1664 and renamed the settlement in honor of the Scottish title of the Duke of York. Albany was chartered in 1686 and became the state capital in 1797. In the late 18th and 19th centuries it was a center of trade and transportation and the original eastern terminus of the [[Erie Canal]].

Family of large [[Seabird|seabirds]] in the order [[Procellariiformes]]. Albatrosses range widely over the [[Southern Ocean]] and the North Pacific and are absent from the North Atlantic except as occasional vagrants. Great albatrosses have wingspans reaching 2.5–3.5 m and are among the largest flying birds. They soar efficiently over long distances and feed on [[Squid|squid]], [[Fish|fish]] and [[Krill|krill]], nesting in colonies on remote oceanic islands. A Laysan albatross named Wisdom, first banded in 1956, is the oldest known wild bird. Of the 22 species recognized by the IUCN, 21 are of some conservation concern. Longline fishing poses the greatest threat, as birds are attracted to baited hooks and drown, and introduced rats and feral cats attack eggs, chicks and nesting adults.

Fraction of [[Sunlight|sunlight]] diffusely reflected by a body, on a scale from 0 to 1. Albedo is 0 for a black body that absorbs all incident radiation and 1 for a body that reflects all of it. Ocean surfaces and most forests have low albedos, while fresh [[Snow|snow]] has a visible-light albedo of about 0.9 to 0.95. Most land areas have albedos between 0.1 and 0.4. Earth's average albedo of about 0.3 is far higher than the ocean's, largely because of clouds. Ice–albedo feedback, in which changes in ice cover alter surface albedo and temperature, plays an important role in [[Climate change|global climate change]]. Earth's surface albedo is estimated from satellite sensors such as the MODIS instruments of [[NASA]].

American experimental physicist. Michelson is known for his measurements of the [[Speed of light|speed of light]] and for the [[Michelson–Morley experiment]], which he carried out with Edward Morley in 1887 and which failed to detect the luminiferous ether. He developed an improved interferometer and used astronomical interferometers to measure stellar diameters and the separations of binary stars. Michelson founded the physics departments of the Case School of Applied Science and the [[University of Chicago]], where he was the first head of the department. He received the 1907 Nobel Prize in Physics, becoming the first American to win a Nobel Prize in science.

Canadian-American psychologist. Bandura taught at [[Stanford University]] from 1953 until becoming professor emeritus in 2010. He originated social learning theory, social cognitive theory and the concept of self-efficacy, the belief in one's ability to succeed in specific situations. His Bobo doll experiment (1961) showed that children who watched an adult act aggressively toward a doll were more likely to do the same, demonstrating observational learning. Through concepts such as reciprocal determinism, his work helped move psychology from [[Behaviorism|behaviorism]] toward [[Cognitive psychology|cognitive psychology]]. A 2002 survey ranked him the fourth most frequently cited psychologist of all time, and he became the first psychologist with more than a million Google Scholar citations.

French philosopher, writer and political activist. Camus was born in French Algeria to pied-noir parents and studied philosophy at the University of Algiers. During World War II he joined the French Resistance and became editor-in-chief of the outlawed newspaper *Combat*. His novel *The Stranger* and his essay *The Myth of Sisyphus* are central works of [[Absurdism|absurdism]], a philosophy his views helped to shape, although he rejected the label existentialist. He received the 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature at the age of 44, the second-youngest laureate. He opposed [[Joseph Stalin]] and the [[Soviet Union]] for their totalitarianism, and during the [[Algerian War]] (1954–1962) he advocated a multicultural and pluralistic Algeria, a position most parties rejected.

American psychologist and psychotherapist. Ellis founded rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT), which holds that irrational beliefs underlie emotional distress, and is regarded as one of the originators of the cognitive revolution in psychotherapy and of cognitive-behavioral therapies. He earned MA and PhD degrees in [[Clinical psychology|clinical psychology]] at [[Columbia University]] and founded the New York City–based Albert Ellis Institute, which he led. He wrote over 80 books and 1,200 articles. In a 1982 survey of American and Canadian psychologists, he was ranked the second most influential psychotherapist in history, behind [[Carl Rogers]] and ahead of [[Sigmund Freud]].

English actor. Finney trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art and became a film star in the early 1960s after his first film, *The Entertainer* (1960), directed by Tony Richardson. His films include *Saturday Night and Sunday Morning* (1960), *Tom Jones* (1963), *Murder on the Orient Express* (1974), *Erin Brockovich* (2000) and the James Bond film *Skyfall* (2012). He received five Academy Award nominations, four for Best Actor. He won several awards for his portrayal of [[Winston Churchill]] in the television film *The Gathering Storm* (2002).

American [[Serial killer|serial killer]]. Born Hamilton Howard Fish, he committed at least three child murders between 1924 and 1928 and was suspected of at least 10 murders. Police arrested him on December 13, 1934, after tracing stationery from a letter he had sent to the mother of Grace Budd, a girl he had kidnapped and murdered. He was convicted and executed in the [[Electric chair|electric chair]].

German architect and Nazi official. Speer joined the [[Nazi Party]] in 1931 and became a close associate of [[Adolf Hitler]], designing the Reich Chancellery and the Nazi rally grounds at [[Nuremberg]]. As Reich Minister of Armaments and War Production from 1942, he greatly increased German war production, relying heavily on slave labor. Convicted at the [[Nuremberg trials]] of war crimes and crimes against humanity, he served 20 years in prison. His postwar memoirs portrayed him as an apolitical technocrat who denied knowledge of the Holocaust. Historians have challenged that account; Martin Kitchen argued that Speer was intimately involved in the [[Final Solution]].

Province of western Canada, one of the three prairie provinces. Alberta is bordered by [[British Columbia]] to the west, [[Saskatchewan]] to the east, the Northwest Territories to the north and the U.S. state of Montana to the south. Canada's fourth-largest province by area, at 661,848 sq km, it has [[Edmonton]] as its capital and [[Calgary]] as its largest city. [[Petroleum]] dominates its economy and exports, and major oil reserves were discovered in 1947. The Alberta Act created the province in 1905. Alberta has six UNESCO World Heritage Sites, including the Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks.

Peruvian politician, president of Peru from 1990 to 2000. He pursued free-market reforms and presided over a campaign against the Shining Path that halted the insurgency but killed thousands of civilians. In 1992 he dissolved Congress and the judiciary in a self-coup, criticized by many politicians but welcomed by much of the business sector. Supporters credit him with stabilizing the economy and ending the insurgency; critics cite the self-coup, corruption and [[Human rights|human rights]] abuses. He fled to Japan in 2000 and sent his resignation by fax, which Congress rejected before removing him from office. He was extradited from Chile in 2007 and sentenced to 25 years in prison.

Swiss sculptor, painter and draftsman. Giacometti is considered one of the most important sculptors of the 20th century. From 1922 he lived and worked mainly in Paris, and his early work was influenced by [[Cubism]] and [[Surrealism]]. He left the Surrealist group in 1935 to concentrate on figures drawn from life. From 1938 to 1944 his sculptures were no more than 7 cm high, reflecting the distance between him and his model. After World War II he produced his best-known works, extremely tall, slender figures that explore isolation and existential themes. Painting formed a small part of his output, and his late paintings are almost monochrome.

German painter, printmaker and theorist of the Northern Renaissance. Born in [[Nuremberg]], Dürer gained a reputation across Europe in his twenties through high-quality woodcut prints. He later preferred engraving and also produced altarpieces, portraits, self-portraits and watercolors. He was in contact with Italian artists including [[Raphael]], Giovanni Bellini and [[Leonardo da Vinci]], and from 1512 he was patronized by Emperor Maximilian I. His introduction of classical motifs and the nude into Northern art, and his treatises on [[Perspective (graphical)|linear perspective]] and body proportions, secured his place among the major figures of the Northern Renaissance. His theoretical writings also covered human anatomy and fortification.

Collection of audio recordings issued on compact disc, vinyl, tape or digitally. Albums dominated recorded music for much of the late 20th century. Early albums were sets of 78 rpm records bound like photo albums. The long-playing vinyl record, introduced in 1948, held about 45 minutes of music and set the pattern for later formats, including the [[Cassette tape|cassette]] and the [[Compact disc|compact disc]]. Most albums are made in recording studios, where separate takes are mixed together. Albums also include live recordings and compilations.Since the 2010s, sales have shifted to downloads and streaming services such as [[Spotify]].

Most populous city in New Mexico (pop., 2020: 564,559), on the [[Rio Grande]]. Founded in 1706 as La Villa de Alburquerque, it was an outpost on El Camino Real linking Mexico City with the northern territories of [[New Spain]]. Kirtland Air Force Base, the largest installation in the Air Force Global Strike Command, is located in the city, as is Sandia National Laboratories. The Albuquerque International Balloon Fiesta is the largest balloon festival in the world.

Small island in San Francisco Bay, California, offshore from [[San Francisco]]. Developed in the mid-19th century with a [[Lighthouse|lighthouse]], [[Fortification|military fortifications]] and a military prison, the island became the Alcatraz Federal Penitentiary in 1934. Strong tidal currents and cold water made escape nearly impossible, and the prison closed in 1963. Native American activists occupied the island for more than 19 months beginning in November 1969. It is part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area and a National Historic Landmark, and it attracts nearly 1.4 million visitors annually.

Ancient protoscientific tradition of natural philosophy, practiced in China, India, the Muslim world and Europe. Western alchemy is first attested in texts written in Greco-Roman Egypt during the first few centuries AD. Common aims included transmuting base metals such as [[Lead|lead]] into [[Gold|gold]], creating an elixir of immortality and finding a panacea for disease. Islamic and European alchemists developed laboratory techniques and terms that are still in use. In 12th-century Europe, translations of Arabic works gave rise to a Latin alchemical tradition that contributed to early modern [[Chemistry|chemistry]] and medicine. Modern historians distinguish between alchemy's practical applications and its esoteric, spiritual aspects.

Athenian statesman and general. A student of [[Socrates]] from the Alcmaeonid family, Alcibiades had [[Pericles]] as one of his guardians. During the [[Peloponnesian War]] he changed allegiance several times. He advocated the Sicilian Expedition, fled to [[Sparta]] after charges of sacrilege, advised the Spartans, then served the Persian satrap Tissaphernes before being recalled to [[Athens]]. Once restored, he won several victories, often by treachery or negotiation rather than siege. Scholars have argued that the Sicilian expedition might have fared better under his command than under Nicias. After enemies exiled him a second time, he was assassinated, reportedly at the instigation of Lysander of Sparta.

Class of organic compounds with at least one hydroxyl (−OH) group bonded to a saturated carbon atom. Alcohols range from simple compounds such as [[Methanol|methanol]] and [[Ethanol|ethanol]] to complex ones such as sugar alcohols and [[Cholesterol]]. The hydroxyl group makes them hydrophilic and provides a site for many chemical reactions. The word derives from Arabic *al-kuḥl*, the name of a powdered [[Antimony]] compound used as eyeliner. Its meaning was later extended to distilled substances in general and then narrowed to ethanol. By the end of the 13th century, distilled alcohol was widely known among Western European chemists.

Active ingredient in beer, wine and distilled spirits, chemically called ethanol. Alcohol is a [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]] depressant that reduces neuronal activity in the brain, producing euphoria, reduced anxiety, sedation and impaired memory and motor function. It is [[Addiction|addictive]], and long-term heavy use is linked to [[Liver|liver]] disease, cardiovascular disease and cancers. The [[World Health Organization]] stated in 2023 that no safe amount of alcohol consumption for cancers and health can be established. Alcohol is the second-most consumed psychoactive drug after [[Caffeine]], and it is legal in most countries but restricted by minimum drinking ages and drunk-driving laws. Humans have produced and consumed it for at least 13,000 years.

Behavioral and physical changes caused by recent consumption of alcohol. Intoxication at lower doses causes mild sedation and poor coordination. Higher doses produce slurred speech, impaired vision, mood swings and vomiting, and extreme doses can cause respiratory depression, coma or death. Intoxication is often defined legally as a blood alcohol concentration above 25–80 mg/dL (0.025–0.080%). [[Acetaldehyde|Acetaldehyde]], a metabolite of alcohol, contributes to the hangover that may follow hours after drinking. Management is supportive, including keeping the person in the recovery position, keeping them warm and ensuring that breathing is sufficient. Gastric lavage and activated charcoal have not been found useful.

Continued drinking of alcohol despite the problems it causes. Also called alcohol use disorder, it is characterized by increased tolerance, physical dependence and withdrawal symptoms when drinking stops. Heavy long-term use can damage the brain, heart, liver, [[Pancreas|pancreas]] and [[Immune system|immune system]], and can cause [[Cirrhosis|cirrhosis]], [[Dementia|dementia]] and Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome. The [[World Health Organization]] estimated that 283 million people had alcohol use disorders in 2016. Genetics and environment are each thought to contribute equally, and a person with a parent or sibling with the disorder is 3–4 times more likely to develop it. Treatment may include [[Benzodiazepine|benzodiazepines]] during withdrawal, acamprosate or naltrexone to reduce cravings, and [[Support group|support groups]] such as Alcoholics Anonymous, which a 2020 review linked to higher abstinence than other clinical interventions.

Red giant star, the brightest in the constellation [[Taurus (constellation)|Taurus]]. Aldebaran lies about 67 [[Light-year|light-years]] away and is typically the 14th-brightest star in the night sky. It is over six billion years old and has evolved off the [[Main sequence|main sequence]]; its radius is about 45 times that of the Sun, while its mass is about equal. Its name derives from the Arabic for 'the follower', because it seems to follow the [[Pleiades]]. It lies along the line of sight to the [[Hyades (star cluster)|Hyades cluster]] but is much older and unrelated to it. Aldebaran forms a [[Binary star|binary]] system with a much fainter companion, Aldebaran B.

Organic compound containing the functional group R–CH=O. The aldehyde carbon is bonded to oxygen by a double bond and to hydrogen and one other substituent, which makes the group polar. [[Formaldehyde|Formaldehyde]] and [[Acetaldehyde|acetaldehyde]] are soluble in water, and the volatile aldehydes have pungent odors. Large-scale production relies on the hydroformylation of alkenes and on the oxidation of [[Methanol|methanol]] and [[Ethanol|ethanol]]. Most sugars, including [[Glucose|glucose]], are derivatives of aldehydes. Aldehydes also contribute to the pleasant odors of essential oils, including cinnamaldehyde and vanillin. They are readily oxidized to [[Carboxylic acid|carboxylic acids]], which distinguishes them from [[Ketone|ketones]].
